summary: Most owners call it a machine that lasts for years and millions of meters with little more than chain oiling and cleaning, and parts are cheap and easy to replace. Complaints are minor: some noise from the flywheel or chain, a hard seat, and the occasional faulty unit on arrival. Used ones are a popular way in.

Most owners find the cables very smooth and the build solid, and many like how much it fits into a rack's footprint. The main downsides are cable twisting for some, plus damaged shipments, missing parts and other quality control problems. Shorter 80-inch racks limit lat pulldown stretch, and the 4-post version needs j-cups removed to use the side trolleys.

Most owners describe it as built like a tank, smooth, and easy to jump on for long steady rides or hard intervals, with many millions of meters and few problems. The stock seat is the most common gripe, and some units had squeaks, clicks, failed pedals or flaking coating. It has no gears or resistance control and is awkward to ride out of the saddle.

Most owners find it solid, stable and easy to move, with upright storage and a grippy pad that beats cheaper benches. Complaints are mixed: some had defective units that REP replaced, and a number wished for a steeper seat angle for incline work or more back angles. A few find the pad gap or attachment range lacking.

Most owners love the solid all-metal build, quick weight changes and compact size at heavy weights, and say they feel like real dumbbells. The main downside is plates sticking in the cradle when racked, which many fixed by adjusting it and some never solved. Some also notice rattling and clanking, and the price is high.

Most owners find it very sturdy and stable, often unbolted, and a good base for REP's attachments such as cables and the Smith. Complaints are few: a couple received scratched parts or clear coat rust marks, which REP replaced or refunded.

Owners like it as a compact, smooth functional trainer, often wall-mounted or on a rack, and several chose it over the Ares to save space. Complaints are few: a couple report fit or build problems, and one finds the stacks light for pulldowns. Reviews are mostly positive but the sample is small.

Owners praise the very solid, tank-like build and the feel of real dumbbells with good knurling and no rattle. The main complaint is slow weight changes, which led some to sell them or find them tedious for circuits. A heavy handle kit is widely recommended, so they suit heavy lifters who change weights rarely.

Mostly positive, with owners calling it effective and durable, even in hot or damp garages. It takes time to learn, and several had early elbow pain that went away with better technique. A few find it less enjoyable than the rower or bike for long sessions.

Owners are very happy with it, calling it solid and stable even unbolted in 3-post or half-rack setups, and it works well with REP attachments. Complaints are minor, such as a little wobble during pull-ups in one 6-post setup. Several mention REP is phasing the series out.

Owners love it as an all-in-one rack, praising smooth cables, a solid Smith and plenty of attachments for the space it uses. The most common gripe is the wobbly sliding bench, and a few had parts break or cables twist, which Force USA support addressed. Assembly cable routing was hard for one.

Owners agree it is very solid and stable, built like a tank. The main downside is the weight, which makes it hard to move, and a few would pick the lighter Nighthawk or a cheaper bench. Suits those who rarely move it, or tall lifters needing the size.

Owners like the fast dial adjustment and the space saved, and several have used them daily for many years without problems. Downsides are the plastic feel, rattling in the tray, and the full-length handle feeling clunky at light weights. One set broke internally after drops.

Owners generally find it solid and commercial-feeling, good for leg press, hack squats and calf raises in a small footprint. Downsides are the low angle needing lots of plates, small foot plates on older versions, and long back-order waits. A couple received damaged or rocking units.

Owners like these for being compact, saving a lot of space and money compared with a set of fixed dumbbells, with a nice grip and a sensible length at light weights. Downsides are some clanking from metal on metal and a couple of units with fit or finish problems. Reviews are limited.

Owners like the grippy knurling that doesn't tear hands, and several prefer it to the Rogue Ohio Power Bar. Complaints are about finish: some marring on Duracoat sleeves, rust on a stainless one, and uneven knurling on one. Mostly positive from a small set of reviews.
